title: Networked music performance
text:
One of the earliest examples of a networked music performance experiment was the 1951 piece: “Imaginary Landscape No. 4 for Twelve Radios” by composer John Cage.[1] The piece “used radio transistors as a musical instrument. The transistors were interconnected, thus influencing each other.”[1,2]

In the late 1970s, as personal computers were becoming more available and affordable, groups like the League of Automatic Music Composers began to experiment with linking multiple computers, electronic instruments, and analog circuitry to create novel forms of music.[3]

The 1990s saw several important experiments in networked performance. In 1993, The University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute began experimenting with networked music performance over the Internet.[4]The Hub (band), which was formed by original members of The League of Automatic Composers, experimented in 1997 with sending MIDI data over Ethernet to distributed locations. However, “ it was more difficult than imagined to debug all of the software problems on each of the different machines with different operating systems and CPU speeds in different cities”.[3] In 1998, there was a three-way audio-only performance between musicians in Warsaw, Helsinki, and Oslo dubbed “Mélange à trois”.[5] The early distributed performances all faced problems such as network delay, issues synchronizing signals, echo, and troubles with the acquisition and rendering of non-immersive audio and video.[4]

The development of high-speed internet over provisioned backbones, such as Internet2, made high-quality audio links possible beginning in the early 2000s.[1] One of the first research groups to take advantage of the improved network performance was the SoundWIRE group at Stanford University's CCRMA.[6] That was soon followed by projects such as the Distributed Immersive Performance experiments,[4] SoundJack,[1] and DIAMOUSES.[7]
